section—I intend to confine my remarks to that sec-
tion—we are bound to enact this provision into law,
because every act that is done to benefit the navigation
of this country benefits all the interests of the country in
its ultimate effects, by its effects upon rights that
are transported between this and other countries. How
the cost of freights is determined. The senator from Ken-
tucky, Mr. UNDERWOOD, has asked, and fairly asked,
what the effect upon his constituency, what is the in-
come of the grower of tobacco, corn, pork, and other
agricultural products, in this action in regard to the
shipping interest of this country. Now, if we were not
satisfied that the interests of the great agricultural portion
of the nation concerned in the passage of this bill,
we should comparatively but little whether passed
not, and if it could operate adversely to that interest,
we would oppose it; for although we consider the shipping
interest a vast interest, still we consider that the agricultural
interest is much vaster and its welfare must be consulted
by us in endeavoring to make the change that we are
now proposing to make. The first mode in which we
find out what supports, what deter-
mines the rates of freight is the proportion between
the quantity of shipping to carry the freight and the
quantity of freight to be carried. And how is that
affected? Everything that benefits your navigating in-
terest, everything that makes the freight of your mer-
chants easier, cheaper and safer in its carriage, will
produce its beneficial effect. You cannot add a thousand
to your shipping without bringing down the rates of
your freight. You cannot impose upon your ship-
owners any liability without rais-
ing your rates of freight, at all events preventing their
reduction. The proportion may be very small; but so far
the effect goes, it will effect upon him whose freight
is carried, but not ultimately upon the ship-owner. He
first feels the benefit of this change, but how long does he
feel it? Just so long as it takes to build more ships and
restore the proportion between the profit made out of that
trade and the profit of other branches of industry and
business. Capital seeks investment in the shape or
shapes that are supposed to be the most profitable, and
when you build ships then down go the rates of
freight, and tobacco and pork and corn are carried
cheaper than before. Is there any escape from that
reasoning? I am really unable to discover any.


Now, sir, the senator from Kentucky has made one re-


pose apply to this question now before us. He says,
how do we know this competition between our shipping
and the shipping of other nations is going on disad-
vantageously to shipping? How do we know that they
are enabled to outdo us, and how do we know that
shipping interests require this relief? When Great
Britain discovered that her shipping required this relief,
she undertook it; and what did she intend to do? She
intended to increase the balance, and cause it to preponder-
ate in her favor, and she intended to keep the ad-
vantage—and do not complain of her, she had per-


fect right to do so; she intended to enjoy the advantages
which her shipping had, and her acts
so far as they tended to give her shipping the adj-
vantage of ours. Now, we do not allow our shipowners
to be subject to this old rule, when another is
found to work fairly there, and we to send our
ships in competition with Great Britain under this dis-
paragement. The competition now is a serious one, and
your returns show it. Here is before me the table of
clearances from ports the last year. The tonnage of
American vessels 2,632,900 tons, while the tonnage of
foreign vessels 720,900 tons, showing that there was
about three-fourths as much foreign tonnage as there is
of domestic. They wish to outdo us. Why do
these vessels in ports bring products which our
American vessels might bring? Well, why do they
carry away products that American vessels might carry
away as well, unless it is that they can ship cheaper
than we can? If they do not carry freight to precisely
the same extent that we do, yet they employ
much, and think that that three-fourths is an
and should be a warning to us. It shows that there is com-
petition against which we ought carefully to guard, and
in removing this burden from the American shipping,
I think we do but act of justice which is called for by the
previous ships which Great Britain has taken, and
called for not only for the benefit of the shipowner, but
for the benefit of those who will ultimately reap the
benefit—that all who benefited directly or indirectly
by the transportation of the freight, as well as the owner
of the goods that are to be carried.


Well sir, it is said that the old rule of the common
law is an old and venerable rule and ought not to be
broken upon. Why, sir, the reasons that led to the
adoption of that rule were not commercial reasons. It was
adopted and applied to common carriers upon land.
Now, whether it is a just rule with regard to the com-
mon carriers upon land, I do not propose to consider; it is
sufficient for this to settle this question. The
why this rule should be applied rather to carriers
upon land than the common carriers upon the water is,
that the danger of breaking the rule is not the same in
the one case as in the other. How can a shipowner to
endanger and risk the property of others that he may
have to carry without endangering his own property by
the negligence or want of integrity? How can he to
do without a risk the destruction of his own prop-
erty? How can his agents that are upon the ships, the
captain and crew, risk the property of others that the
ship owner may have placed under their care, without
great danger to their lives? That is not the
case with the common carrier upon the land. He can risk
the property of others without there being risk to his
own person. Not with the ship owner; for then his
ships would be in danger. There is the ship Typhoon,
Mr. President, that launched last week in Ports-
mouth, in your own State, New Hampshire—(Mr. Nelson,
being in the chair)—which is worth 100,000; if
the crew of that ship put negligent persons, or fraudu-
lent persons upon board of her, who will allow her to
be ashore, be destroyed intentionally by her, or in
any other way to be exposed to danger, it is an easy
matter to allow a ship to be destroyed by fire on a
long voyage without risking the lives of those who, by
their negligence or intentions, permit that destruction
to take place. Now, here are so many reasons why we
are quite safe to relax this rule in the case of
shipping, when it may be safe and advisable to go in the
case of common carriers upon the land.


There are other reasons which occur to me that would
control my mind if these were not sufficient to control
me. But these few ideas seem sufficient to give the rea-
sons for my remarks, and I have thrown them out perhaps in
doing so, taking up much of the time of the Senate.


I am justified in concluding, considering the short time
that remains.

Oregon and her Prospects.

The Albany Argus has received a letter from Capt. Jones, U. S. Army, from Fort Vancouver, under date of October 20, of which the following is an extract:

MANY portions of Oregon are truly beautiful—the valley of the Columbia and of the Willamette river, Puget's Sound, and Astoria Bay, which I have seen, and many other localities, which I hear from the description of my friends. Everything here is rapidly progressive; even during the year that I have been here the changes and improvements have been very great, and in nothing more than in the intercommunication with the Atlantic States. When we arrived here in October, 1849, we glided along this river in batteaux, or in their snake-like canoes, hugging every nook and bay to avoid the strong currents. Now the passing of the steamers warns us of greater Los Yankees. Towns are born of a day, and so rapid are the changes about us that we seem to exist in panorama. A few days since there sat upon my piazza, gazing at Mount Hood, covered with snow Col. Smith, Maj. Orden, and Capt. Leadbetter, engineers; Captains Goldborough and Van Brunt, and Lieutenant Blunt, U. S. Navy, and some dozen JUNIOR officers. The United States steamer Massachusetts and mail steamer Carolina are moored within twenty rods of us. A month since we dined on fresh salmon from Puget's Sound, and had for dessert watermelon from Honolulu as large as a half-bushel. We are now issuing to our troops potatoes from New South Wales, (Sydney) bought by the quartermaster because so much cheaper than could be purchased of the farmers here.

Four hundred emigrant wagons have arrived in Oregon this fall, and six hundred more are on their way. The surplus population of California is also vending this way. There is no measure to the misery existing there now, and the only alternative to the disappointed gold seekers who are destitute but industrious is to come and settle upon the rich farming lands of Oregon. These lands are easily cultivated, and the market for their productions the best, at this time, in the world.

There is no such thing as quiet in Oregon life; all is excitement.

Splendid Vehicle for the Emigrant.

Mr. George Watson, coach maker of Philadelphia, has just completed one of the most exquisite pieces of work, that has ever been accomplished in this country, which he designs to send to the World's FAIR in London. It is a buggy, constructed entirely of American materials, and after original designs prepared expressly for it. The wood, iron, silver plating, silk lining, leather and trimmings, are all of American manufacture.

The running part of the vehicle is of American hickory, beautifully finished. The body is of American walnut, most brilliantly polished and finished as elegantly as the choicest drawing room furniture. The fore part of the coupling presents an American eagle in full flight, exquisitely carved in hickory. The plated ornaments about the vehicle represent the American eagle and the British lion in juxtaposition. The STITCHING, which is all done with the most perfect neatness, represents the device of hands interlocked, emblematic of the cordial friendship existing between the two nations. There are also ornaments representing the American oak and laurel, intertwined with the rose, the thistle, and the shamrock; and in every part there is some pleasing device to remind the spectator of the harmony that exists between the American Republic and the British Empire.

Besides being entirely of American materials, the ornamental work of his fine carriage is all after original designs prepared for it in Mr. Watson's establishment; the dies for the METAL work being cut expressly for it.

the age and how many checks Christian civilization
opposes to the barbarism that this edict would bring
back upon us.

conducted his case with great ability. Several medical

physiology, testified that they regarded Bolding as chief

sumption in favor of his freedom, under Southern
law and in any other kind, the accused would
have the benefit of the doubt. Here proper case

required to prove that the mother of Bolding was a
slave. But no; the Commissioner decides from the
opinion of unscientific men, that Bolding has negro blood
in his veins, and from the fact that he has been for
twenty years a slave, infers that his mother must have
been a slave. So he delivers him to the claimant with
the charitable assurance that any mistake be cor-

might have brought the defendant before him 'without
any warrant whatever' and the investigation would
have been conducted in precisely the same manner;—

citizens being seized without warrant?

joint claimant of Bolding, and that other white men,
who trace their origin to New England but have busi-

swear away his natural liberty. To what pitch of

vation of the community under its influence of the

such deeds are perpetrated in the name of the law
and while any among us retain their honor, their patriotism

repealed or has become a dead letter, or till the system

has come to a different issue from that reported last
week. Judge Conkling declared him entitled to his
freedom, and he has gone to Canada. This decision is
in accordance with law and precedent. Yet the Com-

CRUEL DESERTION.—A little boy, about
2 years of age, was found dead on Sunday
afternoon at the Office of the Commissioner of Emigra-
tion, where he was deserted. The person who
brought him there, whether the child was living
at the time, was not ascertained. The name and whereabouts of the person
who left him there, is also unknown, although every
effort has been used to ascertain it. The body, was re-
spected where the Coroner held an inquest, and the cause of his death, being one of neglect of the child's wants and of lack of
proper care and nourishment, was rendered by the
Jury.


ATTEMPT TO COMMIT SUICIDE.—An
Englishman, 35 years of age, named Wm Kerr, re-
siding in Hudson near Janesville, on Sunday night
cut his throat with razor in horrible manner,
nearly severing the jugular vein. Physicians were
immediately called in and temporarily relieved the
unfortunate man by stopping the flow of blood.
But little hopes are however, entertained of his re-
covery. He has for some days past been much de-
pressed in mind, but no apprehensions were entered
by his friends of his making attempt to destroy his life. He was on TUESDAY removed to
the N. Y. Hospital.

Mr. Simeon Baldwin replied to this address, as
follows:


I am too deeply sensible of the great honor
conferred upon me, and too EMBARRASSED by this dem-
onstration and by all its surrounding circumstances,
to adequately express my feelings on THIS occasion:


You, Sir, have been pleased to eulogize in terms of
approval the part I have taken in the organization
and in the extension of the ASSOCIATION whose an-
niversary we this day celebrate, and which has with
characteristic American progress, advanced in the
short period of seven years from small band of
thirteen original confederates to become grand
National phalanx, spread over and throughout
these United States, and numbering its tens of
thousands.


If I have done anything worthy of commendation
in the structure of this great work, it has been
prompted by my hearty approval of the objects and
CONVICTION of the necessity for such an org-
anization as the Order of United Americans. And
while I have been impelled to active efforts for
the causes and by my natural love for the princi-
ples of American Liberty, and an ardent desire for
its perpetuation and extension, I cannot claim that my
humble exertions are worthy of the
high encomiums you have been pleased to bestow.


Having been placed by the kind favors of the
brothers in various official positions, it has been my
duty to carry out plans designed by them, and if
any merit is due for such plans, it is due to others
and not to him who was only their INSTRUMENT for
promulgating them. To none, Sir, is such credit
more justly due than to yourself, for through all
vicissitudes and trials necessarily attendant on the
organization of this great undertaking, you, sir,
have been a prominent and leading actor, and al-
though some have faltered in their efforts and de-
come weary and faint-hearted, you have been al-
ways ready, and on every necessary occasion your
comprehensive mind has given new impulse to the
work, rushing it toward its high destiny.


I thank the Order for this renewed act of kindness;
they have often placed me under obligations for
official favors, and now that my services have been
deemed worthy of this substantial evidence of their
approval, I have no language to convey to them my
emotions of gratitude.


I accept this splendid memorial of their fraternal
kindness, valuable for its intrinsic worth, more val-
uable in its conception, as a treasure of inestimable value
which shall preserve and transmit to my children
an heirloom emblematic of that glorious legacy of
our patriot forefathers, to be cherished by men, as
we by our Order, would cherish and MAINTAIN the
glorious liberties they bequeathed to us.

MR. EDITOR Your paper being devoted
to the advocacy of sound morals as well as
politics, I have expected before this to see
some notice in it of the action taken by the
legislature of Illinois on the subject of Tem-
perance. But presuming that it has escaped
your eye in the selection of news for the pub-
lic, I take pleasure in furnishing the main
principles of the bill as it passed in that body.


1. It repeals all present License laws.


2. Prohibits the sale of intoxicating drinks
in less quantity than one quart, under pen-
alty of $25.


3. If sold to minors increases the fine to
from $40 to $100.


4. Provides for penalty of not less than
$25, nor $500, for selling more than a quart,
and permitting the same to be drunk on the
premises of the seller.


5. Giving away liquor, to come within the
provision of the law.


While we regard this action as a great ad-
vance in the public sentiment of that state on
this subject, and as indicative of a spirit
which should fill all of our legislative bodies;
we must still consider the bill faulty in seve-
ral particulars, though admirable in others. —
The first clause is right and just, for we have
ever been unable to appreciate the argu-
ments why there should be a privileged class
in a community licensed to retail misery and
pauperism on the industrious. If a bless-
ing, why should not all enjoy the privilege?
The second will have tendency to prevent
drunkard-making, for a man has gone far
down the hill when he will turn into a grog-
shop and purchase a quart of whiskey for his
own drinking. Perhaps the reason why they
did not make the quantity greater than
a quart was, they intended to kill off all the
old drunkards as fast as possible, which if re-
garded in a pecuniary point of view alone, is
certainly desirable. We think that or 10
gallons would have been better. The third,
in relation to minors is highly commendable,
but the penalty should be more severe, for it
is from the young that our army of drunkards
is recruited. The fourth is good in some of
its specifications but defective in others.
The amount to be sold may do; but why not
compel the buyer to drink it on the premises
instead of carrying it away and disturbing
his peaceful and sober neighbors, and hold
the seller responsible for his conduct while
under his influence? The fifth clause of the
bill must bear with great weight on the mer-
chants of Illinois, especially if they deal
their customers with whiskey as their brethren
do in this portion of the Union.


One should have been pleased to see
a feature in this bill similar to what has
become law in the state of Wisconsin.
There the retailer of liquors is held respon-
sible for the good conduct of his customers,
and is required to give heavy bonds for the
same. The only testimony needed for his
conviction, is that of the wife, or single
competent individual in the community who
will swear that the person prosecuted has
sold liquor to the trespasser on the public
peace within three days. If that is proven,
the seller is held responsible for all damages
and he has the privilege of suing a suit
against his plaintiff in the same honorable
fashion, for their proportion of the fine. The
practical scouring of this law among the fra-
ternity is both amusing and instructive; and
I cannot compare it to anything on land;
and therefore, must seek a comparison in the
ocean, where the larger sharks devour the
smaller. When will we so far advance in
morality and happiness as to enact similar laws
in the Keystone State?

To the Editors of The Courier and Enquirer.

I have this day received by mail a narrative of one James Marks, which I am informed was published not only in your paper but also in the Herald and Tribune, in which the following:

Eighty-one Hungarian exiles, who recently arrived from Europe started on Saturday last, from New York, for their future home at New Buda, Governor Ujhazy's settlement in the far western wilds of Iowa, whither they proceed, on the especial recommendation of their great leader and brother in misfortune, Louis Kossuth. For it hath a holy spell;
And the scene that name recalleth

While its passing, will tell.
We are sitting in the twilight

For the first time—he and I.
And no weight of woe is pressing

On our hearts, so heavily;
For the cruel fates have willed it

And the parting hour draws nigh,
While each heart in silence striveth
For the strength to say, "Good-bye"
'Tis in vain, can no longer

Check the outburst of my grief,
And my tears fall thick and heavy

Yet they bring me no relief.
He hath risen, and is standing

With calm unruffled brow,
On his breast his arms lie folded
just as then, I see him now.
Suddenly stilled my weeping,

And my face upturned to meet
Such look of love—so holy

Never mortal eye did greet.
While his hand just touched my forehead,
From his lips in low tones fell
On my heart, so torn with sorrow,
"God, our Father, bless thee Nell"
Years have passed since then, and silent
Is that voice in death and cold;
Turned to dust, the hand that rested
On my brow, now dim and old.
Yet this hour doth ever whisper

O'er again, our last farewell,
And my heart grows still to listen,
"God, our Father, bless Thee Nell"

apparently so near his end; and yet the serene
countenance of the wan invalid was suffused
with a glad, almost holy expression, that soften
ed its ghastliness and made its sadness more
spiritual. Day after day, I passed, met him
always in the same place, either being assisted
by some friend into the old chaise, or sitting so
listless, yet so patient, waiting the progress of
the laborers engaged with their work around
him.


By chance I met a friend who knew the in-
valid. I mentioned carelessly my opinion of his
apparently hopeless case, and wondered, as
any passing stranger would, who he was, and
what drew him so frequently and steadily to
the shop of the marble worker.


"He is a doomed man," replied my compan-
ion, "and being fully aware that his time is short,
he is experimenting the work of his own mon-
ument."


I was startled, and looked my friend fixedly
in the face. "It is a heartless whim," ex-
claimed impatiently, "a living man watching
the progress of his own tombstone!"


"No, not heartless," he replied, "only singu-
lar." George Bennett, that is his name, was
once a young man of good health and good
expectations—but that latter was his
ruin in manner; never a more humble, pa-
tiently waiting heir did I see, sir, than that
same young man; but," he added with emph a-
sis, "when his uncle died, and the splendid for-
tune came—one fortune and no mistake, sir—
he was off and away on the broad road to dis-
sipation. Beginning with moderate prodigali-
ty to rid himself of this golden encumbrance,
his desires soon knew no bounds. He gradually
threw off the restraints which once a sense of du-
ty, engendered by mother's pious teachings,
had kept him under, plunged into fashionable
follies, forgot God, ruined a good constitution,
and soon sank all but a small portion of his
fine legacy. Poor fellow, in his case the race
was to the swift; but it has ended in his destruc-
tion. Now here comes the romance.


In his younger days he really loved, and en-
deared, a gentle girl of Scotch descent, one of the most
amiable creatures I ever knew; but she had
only a few thousands, say three at the most, to
bring as wedding dowry. She never doubt
ed his truth, nor would she believe the least re-
port derogatory to his reputation. Ah well,
but women are loving and forgiving creatures"
soliloquized my friend with an absent air. He
was a bachelor, and for full three minutes he
was silent.


"Did he ever marry her?" I asked with
concealed feeling of impatience.


"Never;" he exclaimed abruptly, "no; he
went to Philadelphia, dangled around a few gold
satellites from thence to Europe, came back to
the States, paid court to a lady of wealth, and
would willingly have wedded her, but did not,
for the very good reason that she learned to de-
spise his character.


After an absence of three years he visited
Boston again, wrecked in body and fortune. I
met him first, and well remember how heavily
he leaned upon my side as we walked together
through the old familiar thoroughfares. He
said nothing about his prospects or disappoint-
ments, but talked of various subjects, mostly of
politics and Europe, till we by merest accident
stood opposite the old ground—you remember,
Copp's Hill.


I forgot to say that I too had been for many
months absent. Bennett expressed a wish to
walk through, and did it not seem strange that
he made pause, from very weakness and wea-
riness, opposite a small, smooth, white stone,
that was familiar to neither of us; and when
I would have led him farther on, he pushed aside
the long, damp grass, and fell to reading the
inscription.


Judge of my surprise, as well as his remorse,
when I read the following:


Sacred to the memory
ALICE GLEN,
